intro: The Manakkula Vinayaka temple is among Pondicherry’s oldest and most revered shrines. Because a large sandy pond (Manarkulam) existed in ancient times where the deity currently resides, a small square sandy pit next to the deity commemorates it now, since the original pond was filled. The fact that water still seeps into this pit to this day is considered a special affirmation of its sacred origin. Once called Bhuvanesa and later Vedapuri Vinayagar, this pre-15th-century temple therefore became known as the Manakkulathu Vinayagar.
Some key recent events in the life of this temple:

1961: When the Sri Aurobindo Memorial Fund Society purchased property to the south of the temple, the Mother of Pondicherry’s Sri Aurobindo Ashram arranged the transfer of a portion on the northern side of the property, by way of gift, to the Manakkula Vinayaka temple to provide space for parikrama. She had a special relationship with Manakkula Vinayaka: “In 1930 we were having regular meditations in the Prosperity hall,” she has said. “At one of these meditations, quite unexpectedly, Ganesh appeared suddenly to my inner view. He was of golden light and surrounded by a very luminous golden aura. His form was the usual one as on his images. It was the first time I ever saw him and I expressed some surprise over his sudden appearance. Then he told me, ‘You see I am a living being quite real and concrete - and to give you a concrete proof of my reality I shall send to you henceforth, all the money you will need.’ And on this promise he disappeared. He has kept his promise for years and the money was coming abundantly.” When Ganesha asked for the temple parikrama space, therefore, the Mother made arrangements for it.

1968: A sphatika (crystal) lingam found on the land of D. Ramachandra Reddiar was donated to the temple in the presence of Lieutenant Governor B.D. Jatti. This sphatika lingam receives a daily abhishekam and a special one on Pradosham days, usually carried out by an elder priest known to us as Delhi Mama.

1977: An elephant named Lakshmi was offered as a donation to this temple in the presence of Puducherry Lieutenant Governor Rajendra Kumari Bajpai. Lakshmi lived in the chariot shed of the Vedapuriswara temple, near the temple kulam, and the sound of her anklets would announce her comings and goings from the Manakkula Vinayaka temple. She died in 2022, and her frequently tended samadhi is on a ground near Golden Bridge Pottery.

1989: A gold foil-covered chariot was presented by Dewan Kandappa Mudaliar and Sabapathi Mudaliar (of the Nandhikeswara temple) to the Manakkula Vinayaka temple. Manakkula Vinayaka comes in this golden chariot to meet Nandhikeswara on specific days of the year.
Sources: Various, and will be outlined in the longer version of this writing, coming soon.

The Sri Tripurasundari Samedha Shri Vedapuriswarar Thirukoyil, or the Vedapuriswara Koyil for short, is one of the two major Siva temples within the town’s boulevards, and the one whose main deity names Pondicherry as “Vedapuri Kshetram.”

The temple is the largest and most important Siva temple in the town, with the Ayira Vysya Chetty community’s Kalatthiswara Koyil being next in size and stature. It is managed jointly with the Varadaraja Perumal Koyil a bare block to the north. The temple complex has several sub-shrines, including ones to Vinayaka, Murugan, Palani Andavar, Balamurugan, Mahalakshmi and Nataraja, alongside several shrines housing additional lingas (Bhaktapuriswara and Kasi Viswanatha being the more important of these). Its kulam is the source of the theertham for the nearby Draupadi Amman Koyil for preparatory pujas during their Aadi Masam Agni Vasanta Vizha. At its rear is the town’s only living nandavanam or temple garden, with a beautiful maha bilvam (a 19 pinnate-leaf variety of the common Aegle marmelos), old and gnarled nochi (Vitex negundo) grown into a tree, and the uncommon thiruvodu (Crescentia cujete) yet to bear fruit. The Siruthonda Nayanar Thiruthondu Sabhai is very active here in propitiating the 63 Nayanmars, and doing Guru pujas on their respective nakshatra-naal or birthdays. Another group is routinely present at the Durga shrine on Tuesdays and other important days, doing parayanam. Still other groups accompany the Palliyarai swami in a palanquin daily at the temple opening with songs, prayers, conch and damaru sounds (Thirupalliyezhucchi), and once again when the deity is returned to his sleeping chamber at the time of the ardhayama puja and the temple’s closing. The temple conducts its Mahotsavam or annual festival in the month of Vaikasi (May-June) each year.

He who emerged from Brahma’s sacrifice, the Lord who dwells atop Hastigiri, the King of Boons and the monarch of Kanchipuram – many are the glories of Varadaraja. Invoking these glories onto the kshetram of Pondicherry is the Sri Perundevi Thayar samedha Sri Varadaraja Perumal Koyil on MG Road, merely one block north of the Vedapuriswara Koyil. Perumal sits in his sanctum with Sridevi and Bhudevi, with Garudalvar facing him. Perumal’s primary consort, Perundevi Thayar, sits in her own shrine in the southern prakaram. The temple also holds Pandarinatha, Andal, Anjaneya, Manavala Mamunigal, Vedanta Desika, and – most belovedly – Kodanda Rama. Inside the Kodanda Rama shrine also sit Venugopala, Navaneetha Krishna and Thavazhthal Kannan, although they are seen only once in the year during Janmashtami.

The alankara-priya, or adornment-adoring Perumal is given ample occasions to be adorned. 282 days of the year are dedicated to one or another utsavam, puja or jayanti! – placing it by far among the most festive temples of the town. The temple follows the Vaikhanasa agamic tradition. It is also said to share the relation of an Abhimana Sthalam with the Divya Desam of Thiruvahindrapuram – that is, it associates itself with the Devanatha Swami temple by following its festival patterns, thus placing itself within the broader network of sacred Vaishnava sites. These festivals are supported not only by long-standing individual families, but also by other groups that have consistently served the temple over the decades. The Sri Kodandaramar Swami Bhakta Jana Sabhai, founded in 1972, has been one such and has been very active in its organisation and contribution to the continuation of the utsavams over the past 50 years. Some other groups are the Desikar, Mamunigal and Pandarinatha groups.

The Kamakshi Amman (or Kamatchi Amman) Koyil on Bharati Street is a Vishwakarma community temple. It is said that when the Vedapuriswara Koyil at the site of the present Immaculate Conception Cathedral was destroyed, members of this community rescued the Ambal figure and consecrated it at their own temple. The story goes that when Parvati once playfully covered the eyes of Siva, the world was plunged into darkness. Fearing Siva’s anger, Parvati descended into the world to perform various penances. Her fiercest ones were in Mangaadu (just west of Chennai), her far more placid seated penance is famously in Kanchipuram, and her standing, placid penance is in Pondicherry. Here the Goddess stands about 5 foot tall. Above her is a 45-foot vimanam; the entrance to her temple is a 5-tiered Rajagopuram, both are built from burnt terracotta. The Murugan-Valli-Devasena and the extraordinary Dakshinamurti in this temple, both in a green-hued granite whose tint is visible only during abhishekams, are both said to have come also from the older, destroyed Vedapuriswara Koyil.

The temple’s major festival is the Kinni Rathotsavam in Chithirai Masam. Its highlight is the pulling of the temple car on the 9th day, which coincides with Chithirai Pournami. A 20 foot-high ther decorated with varying sizes of concave metal disks (resembling kinnams or small cups), polished so that they gleam in the moonlight, gives the festival its name. It also gives the temple its informal name: Kinni Ther Koyil.

The twin complex of Sri Kalatthiswarar-Sri Varadaraja Perumal Devasthanam stands tall on Mission Street at the heart of the Heritage Town, defying all inflictions of time. Built and sustained by the Ayira Vysya Chettiar community, the ‘Chetty Koyil’ holds in its stones the story of an unfaltering continued lineage. At least going as far back as 1693, when it first featured in a Dutch map, but surely in existence for a long time prior, the temple has been a central node around which the town that came to be Pondicherry has grown.

The organisation of two temples within one complex is a heavy undertaking to say the least. The Kalatthiswara-Gnanambigai shrine, invoking no doubt the Kalahastiswara shrine of Andhra Pradesh, houses a Siva Lingam and Ambal in respective sanctums. The Varadaraja Perumal shrine invokes together with the Perumal Koyil on MG Road the great Varadaraja of Kanchipuram. The temple celebrates all the utsavams that the Saiva and Vaishnava traditions entail, including two Pavitrotsavams and, most importantly, two Brahmotsavams. Adding to the count is also the Lada Chinnamman temple on Lally Tollendal Street, which belongs to Chetty Koyil and is used often as a “Keni Kulam”, or temple tank. Soil for the Mrtsangrahana puja is collected from here before any major festivals at the main temple.
During the 1748 Dupleix-Jesuit destruction of the original Vedapuriswara temple, many of the idols found shelter at the Kalatthiswara temple further up the road.

The Draupadi Amman Thirukoyil in Pondicherry’s heritage town is not marked in any old maps, but was known to exist from colonial times. The temple has the dual identity of being a shrine to Dharmaraja (whose name appears along with the Iswaran Koyil on street name plates) and one to Draupadi Amman. Pujas are done by a hereditary Vanniar priest twice daily, with a simple abhishekam in the morning only. A single family has attended to this temple for 10 generations; the last several generations’ photographs hang in the temple’s main foyer. The temple’s main festival is the 25-day Agni Vasanta Thiruvizha, which begins on the Monday following the first Friday of Aadi Masam, and holds its famed theemidi or fire-walking ceremony on the third Friday following. Recitations and storytelling from the Villu Bharatam, a 14th-century Mahabharata retelling in Tamil by Villiputturar, are held daily, in the evenings. Each episode elaborates what the day’s rituals will celebrate or themselves re-enact. Draupadi Amman faces East, though the entrance to her temple faces South.

Sri Vasavi Kannika Parameswari Temple was built in 1921 by the Arya Vysyas of Pondicherry. The main temple of this community is in Penukonda, Andhra Pradesh where the Goddess Sri Vasavi Kannika Parameswari incarnated. The temple features European style columns and arches around the central sanctuary. The moola murti is South facing, as is the temple entrance on Kamakshi Amman Koyil Street, at the MG Road cutting. Immediately outside the garbhagriha, to her right is Vinayaka, and on her left is Murugan. This garbhagriha area is separated by two doors, made distinctive by the presence of coloured stained glass lunettes above them, that lead to the rear prakaram. To their left and right are small rooms, temples in their own right. The right temple has utsava figures of Rama, Lakshmana, Sita, and Hanuman; the left has the utsava murtis of Mahalakshmi, Ganesha, and two large and small Kubera Yantras which were found on the site at the time of the building construction. Being the private temple of the Arya Vysya Chettys or Telugu Komati community, but also the private temple of a community long settled in Tamil-speaking Pondicherry, the Kannika Parameswari temple follows mostly the Tamil calendar, but also the Telugu for some events, such as Ugadi and Vasavi Jayanti. Its key annual events are the 13-day Rama Navami Utsavam in Panguni and a 17-day Navaratri utsavam in Purattasi-Aippasi.

Angala Nagar in Muthialpet gets its name from the ugra goddess who presides over the region. Angalamman is the only “vadaka paatha”, or north-facing Amman, who protects against threats which have historically come from the North. The temple also holds the shrines of Kalkatta Kali, Annapurni, Siva, Rama, Pavadarayan and Pecchayi Amman. This last Pecchayi Amman is the ferocious midwife who rescued the infant-incarnate Siva, and sits always in the dim light of a single lamp. There is also an adjacent Sri Shakti Vinayaka shrine which belongs to the temple. The Kalkatta Kali seems unique to the Angalamman temples, and is worshipped every month on theipirai ashtami, or the ashtami of the waning fortnight. This and the Lawspet Murugan Koyil are the only temples outside the boulevards that we are covering in this project.

The primary utsavam for Angalamman is the re-enactment of the Vallala Kottai followed by the Mayana Kollai. The first is the retelling of the story of Pecchayi Amman’s slaying of King Vallala’s queen, performed with folk instruments, song, and costumes. A large sand-figure of the queen is made and destroyed by a charging array of goddesses who then go on procession. The Mayana Kollai is the re-enactment of Angala Parameswari descending onto the graveyard to free Siva of His Brahmahati, or Brahma-slaying curse. She lures the Kapala from Siva’s hand with food scattered across the graveyard, then reduces it to ashes by stepping upon it with her right foot.

The Mutthumariamman Thirukoyil is one of the oldest Amman shrines in Pondicherry, tended to by two hereditary lineages of pusaris for 9 generations. Pujas are offered twice daily by a hereditary Vanniar priest, with abhishekam only in the morning at temple opening. The deity here is not a Thalai Mariamman or the Mariamman shown just with a head, but a full seated figure. At several times of the year, she receives an abhishekam followed by an elaborate alankaram that can take all night to prepare for the next morning’s puja. The priests pride themselves on developing and growing the alankara traditions of this temple. The temple’s Aandu Vizha or celebration of the anniversary of its last Kumbhabhishekam (2024) occurs at the end of August, in the middle of Aavani Masam. Its annual festival is celebrated in Thai (January-February), inaugurated on the fifth day following Amavasya, each day’s festival is conducted by one of the communities of the town: Dhobi, Senaithalaivar, Naidu, Vysya, Vellala, Vannia, Senguntha Mudaliar, Vanniar, Arya Vysya and Brahmins conduct the festival respectively, with the Dhobis doing the dhvajarohanam and the Brahmins finishing with the unjal utsavam, according to longstanding arrangements. Mutthumariamman is the kuladaivam for local families, many of whom have moved to France but continue to return for key events and/or sponsor them from afar. As such, the temple becomes the site for several private functions, such as the Periyandavar Puja, and the place where all local communities come for Deepavali and Amavasya nonbu (fasting or other related observances).

The Manimutthumariamman Aalayam is a theruvu koyil or a roadside shrine that its devotees say is over a hundred years old. A Brahmin priest performs a puja daily in the mornings, and returns to perform a Friday special abhishekam every week, when the temple nirvagam also does an Annadanam. The temple itself is a building barely large enough to house the main deity, a few utsava murtis and what is needed for their weekly worship. A small prakaram winds around the shrine, to the back of which is the temple’s sthala vriksha–a neem tree, now entwined with a ficus or peepul. Beneath these trees, facing north is a small Kanaka Valli Durgai. Above the temple is a stucco figure of Parashakti, accessible only by ladder. The temple’s only major annual festival is a 3-day celebration: an elaborate homam and dhvajarohanam on Day 1, a karaga vizha or festive event centred on the worship of the Goddess through a sacred pot (karagam), which is ceremonially decorated and carried on the head in procession on Day 2, which concludes with a kumbha padayal and a veethi purappadu or street procession for the Goddess, and a special abhishekam and annadanam on Day 3, followed by an unjal utsavam. Additional priests are called in for these functions, as are pambaikarars (folk percussionists and storytellers) and other village deity ritualists.

Sri Bhavani Amman Aalayam and Sri Sundara Vinayaka Thirukoyil on Bharati Street at the cutting of Thillai Maestry is a family temple established in 1910 by its present owner’s great grandfather, known as Thiru. Rathinasabhapati Guruswamy. Its present ward is Mrs. Rani, the 4th generation of caretakers, with Rajendran sir acting as the officiating priest. The temple itself is a Vinayaka shrine, but there is an independent Bhavani Amman shrine just outside to the left, and a Sundaravadana Krishna shrine to the right. The latter was established by the local Yadava community who used to rent an utsava murti for their Janmashtami festivities, and eventually occupied a portion of the Sundara Vinayaka temple for a full-fledged shrine. The two temples share space, but are independent of each other. Inside, the temple appears to have evolved organically: an aunt helped to establish the Murugan sannadhi (and sponsors the Thirukalyanam on the day following Kanda Sashti), there is an Ayyappa shrine presumably for those wishing to undertake the pilgrimage to Sabarimala in the last part of the English calendar year. It is the only temple in Pondicherry to house and perform bi-monthly pujas to Varahi Amman and the Saptamatrikas. In addition, the temple keeps a number of weekly and monthly rituals, including Pradosham, Krittikai, all the six annual Nataraja abhishekams and so on. Women from the surrounding neighbourhoods are often there, adding voices to the prayer. The temple’s 10-day Brahmotsavam starts a day after Vinayaka Chaturthi, but does not feature veethi purappadu or street processions.

The Siva Subramania Swamy Devasthanam in our documentation represents the temple life of Pondicherry’s Lawspet locality. Along with the Angalamman Koyil of Muthialpet, it is the only other temple that falls outside the confines of the boulevards. The first original shrine of the site was Adi Vinayaka who sits to the left of Murugan, which evolved from Siva Kumara, to Mayil Murugan – both of whom are now at the back – to finally settling on the Siva Subramania Swami. Around the prakaram are shrines to Shanmukha, Palani Andavar, Nava Veerangal, Siva Kumara, Mayil Murugan, Siva Lokanathar and his consort, Valli on the unjal, the Navagrahas, Naalvar and Durga. The temple stands out for its ritual enactments, which seem to always be done with care and deliberation. Further up the road is the Bala Mutthumariamman shrine, which is the temple’s dedicated Amman shrine and is given kaalasandhi puja every day.

The primary festival, like all other Murugan temples, is the Skanda Sashti Soora Samharam which comes immediately after Deepavali. The festival usually lasts seven days with the slaying on the 6th and the divine wedding on the 7th day. The temple has a thanga-ther, or golden chariot which is brought out for ul-purappadu during Panguni Utthiram, Vaikasi Vishakam and the monthly Krittikais. The nearby Veerabhadraswamy temple’s alagu sevai, or knife-festival begins only after performing its initial puja at the Siva Subramania Swami temple.

Born in 1940 in Pondicherry, a Muslim man named Mohammed Ghouse had always felt a special fondness for Lord Murugan. As a boy, he sold the gold waist-thread his parents had tied on him to make small copper idols of Murugan with Valli-Deivanai (Devasena), which he would worship daily. Every year at Masi Maham, he decorated his Murugan and carried the idol to the sea for its theerthavari. Thus did Ghouse’s Murugan come to be called “Bhai Murugar.” Legend has it that Murugan appeared in a dream and asked him to build a temple for him on a specific ground. On 14 December 1970, the foundation stone was laid together with Lieutenant Governor B.D. Jatti. Not everyone found it easy to accept a Muslim building a Hindu temple, but it was completed nonetheless. In 1977, the Maha Kumbhabhishekam was performed and Kanchi Periyavar later named the temple Ghousiga Balasubramania Swami Aalayam, fully acknowledging its founder. Ghouse’s sons and grandson now run the temple, honouring their father’s devotions.

A Thulasi Mutthumariamman shrine already existed nearby, and the temple as we see it today has grown around it, taking the proceedings of this Amman Koyil into its folds. The main temple now houses a number of deities including Panchamukha Anjaneya, Vinayaka, Perumal with Sridevi and Bhudevi, Vaidyanatha Siva, Thaiyal Nayaki Ambal, and several utsava murtis.

Thulasi Mariamman has a dhvajastambha of her own, and her 11-day Brahmotsavam is conducted in Chithirai Masam. The reigning Balasubramania Swami’s major annual festival happens in Aippasi, the 18-day Kanda Sashti, with a 5-day series of events built around Vaikasi Vishakam. Panguni Utthiram is also celebrated with a Thirukalyanam. The popularity of this temple is evident from the crowds that throng there to see the beautiful moola murti on Tuesdays, Krittikai, and Sashti–and, indeed, from the temple’s very active Instagram page.

Arulmigu Sri Manonmani Mariamman Thirukoyil is a tiny family-owned theruvu koyil. It is owned and managed by the family that lives in a yellow building above a series of shops on Canteen Street (between Ambaltadayer Madam St and Nehru St), just across from the shrine. The person who used to officiate or otherwise oversee the temple was a government employee with the Slum Clearance Board, but he passed away in 2026, so his son Vishnu who was once his aide now sometimes takes charge of the alankaram and puja. The family typically hires an Iyer (Brahmin priest) to perform a puja in the mornings, and be present for a period during the sayarakshai time, in the evenings. The elderly grandmother tells us that the deity came from the Senkazhuneer Amman Koyil Kulam (water tank) on Pappammal Koil Street in Vaithikuppam. A Chettiar who lived nearby had brought and consecrated it, but then stopped and placed it in a well in the house of a carpenter nearby, as it is the custom to discard holy images and forms in water bodies rather than leaving them unattended or elsewhere. When the murti resurfaced from the well is when the brother of Shanta’s grandfather took it, installed it in a small space next to his dwelling (where the temple is now), and began pujas to it. So we know from this that the temple as such is approximately 3 generations old. There have been 2 Kumbhabhishekams done, with the help of Ganesh Gurukkal who is now the main priest at the Manakkula Vinayaka temple. The temple’s main festivities occur on Aadi Masam Fridays, with special alankaram for the deity.

The Sri Nandhikeswarar Thirukoyil is located on Vellalar Street near the MG Road area in Pondicherry. This is a 19th-century shrine notable for housing the underground samadhi of its builder and founder, Sri Nadu Shanmuga Velayudha Swamigal, son of the caste chief, agriculturist and interpreter Nadou Sidambara Mudaliar, belonging to the Tondaimandala Vellala community. Nadou Shanmuga Velayudha Mudaliar was an elected member of the Colonial Council created in the interests of allowing more Indians representation in French colonial governance (1872). This staunchly Hindu ancestral lineage has shaped Pondicherry in more ways than one, for example by marshalling resources and donating land on which the Varadaraja Perumal Koyil now stands, and to which the destroyed Vedapuriswara Koyil could then be rebuilt. A gold-plated chariot that had long been in a shed across from the temple was donated by the present Dewan to the Manakkula Vinayaka Koyil, a gesture still acknowledged by the annual visit of Manakkula Vinayaka to Nandhikeswara on Masi Thiruvathirai (Ardra) in that very golden chariot.

The temple has three parts: the Gangai Vinayaka temple, which is the older shrine always open for worship; the samadhi koyil itself, which was established on the Swamigal’s passing; and the Nandhikeswara temple, which became central thanks to his devotions. The temple remained a private shrine, shuttered off by most accounts, and attended to only by the present Dewan’s older brother. But here the Swamigal had wanted to remain always under the feet of the reigning deity; thus was his samadhi placed in the temple basement. The temple initially had a Nataraja-figured Nandi as its main deity, but was advised by members of the Dharmapuram Adheenam that a temple cannot have a pashu (animal) without a pati (lord)–or a Nandi without a Siva–and so the Siddheswara lingam was there consecrated. Nandhikeswara figures in dancing and standing forms remain by his side. A panchaloham Siddheswari followed soon after, and She remains beside Siddheswara only in her utsava form. A Murugan-Valli-Devasena utsava murti is also worshipped here. Since this is a samadhi koyil, Amavasya observances are more important than Pournami celebrations.

The temple is unique in other ways as well: on the dhvajastambha or kodimaram is copper cladding with Tamil beeja mantras on each face; a stone beeja mantra murti sits in between the pole and the Vrushabha. All pujas here are conducted in Tamil; the two young priests, both brothers only here for two years, have had all their training with a Tamil professor at SRM University in Chennai. But their methods of performing both daily and special pujas are exceptionally beautiful. They also have introduced novel alankara methods, evident during major festivals like Navaratri and Kanda Sashti.
